content: 1. It is essential to ensure that the guidelines and policies derived from them respect fundamental human rights. This includes safeguarding the rights of individuals and patients to confidentiality of their information and informed decision-making, in alignment with national ethical guidelines. 2. The target audience for this guideline includes key decision-makers in countries where lymphatic filariasis (LF) is endemic. It aims to assist them in determining if, when, and how to implement alternative mass drug administration (MDA) regimens. The guideline is intended to inform policy on MDA for LF-endemic countries. 3. The primary audience includes coordinators of national programs for controlling and eliminating neglected tropical diseases, managers of national LF elimination programs, and national committees or technical groups that support critical programmatic decisions. It also serves as a reference document for stakeholders supporting the Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis (GPELF), including health ministries, WHO, regional program review groups, technical review bodies, pharmaceutical manufacturers, bilateral donor organizations, non-governmental organizations, and academic institutions. 4. The WHO steering committee developed provisional guideline questions and determined the scope of the guideline. The guideline development group refined these questions further, following the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes) framework. These questions formed the basis for systematic literature reviews and strategies for evidence synthesis. 5. PICO Question 1: Should IDA (ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine, and albendazole) versus DA (diethylcarbamazine and albendazole) be used for annual MDA to eliminate LF in implementation units (IUs) where onchocerciasis is not co-endemic? Outcomes include complete microfilarial clearance, microfilarial density, circulating filarial antigen (CFA), adverse events (AEs) of varying grades, and serious adverse events (SAEs). 6. PICO Question 2: Should biannual DA versus annual DA be used for MDA to eliminate LF in IUs where onchocerciasis is not co-endemic? Outcomes include microfilarial prevalence reduction, CFA reduction, and IgG4 reduction for Brugia species. 7. PICO Question 3: Should IDA versus IA (ivermectin and albendazole) be used for annual MDA to eliminate LF in IUs co-endemic with onchocerciasis? Outcomes include complete microfilarial clearance, microfilarial density, CFA, inactive adult worm nests, AEs, and SAEs. 8. PICO Question 4: Should biannual IA versus annual IA be used for MDA to eliminate LF in IUs co-endemic with onchocerciasis? Outcomes include microfilarial prevalence and CFA reduction. 9. PICO Question 5: Should biannual albendazole versus annual albendazole be used for MDA to eliminate LF in IUs co-endemic with loiasis where ivermectin has not been distributed? Outcomes include microfilarial prevalence reduction and CFA reduction. 10. The WHO guideline development process adhered to the procedures outlined in the 2014 WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach was used to assess evidence quality and formulate recommendations. 11. The systematic review process included a comprehensive review of primary literature, including randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies. The search strategy did not exclude studies based on publication year, status, language, or participant characteristics, ensuring inclusion of ongoing trials. 12. Meta-analyses were conducted to evaluate the efficacy and safety outcomes listed in the PICO questions. The quality of evidence was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool and other criteria such as inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. 13. The guideline development group, formed in January 2017, included 18 members from diverse professional backgrounds, ensuring geographical representation, skill diversity, and gender balance. Their names and affiliations are listed in Annex 3. 14. Potential conflicts of interest were evaluated and managed throughout the guideline development process. All members completed declarations of interest, which were reviewed by WHO. No significant conflicts were identified that would exclude any member from participating fully. 15. The WHO steering committee developed the guideline proposal, including the scope and initial PICO questions. The guideline development group refined these questions, reviewed evidence profiles, and formulated recommendations. 16. The systematic review team ensured that all relevant evidence was critically appraised and synthesized. The guideline methodologist led the evidence-to-decision process, ensuring appropriate application of the GRADE approach. 17. Peer reviewers provided comments to improve clarity and understanding of the guideline. These suggestions were addressed and incorporated into the final document before submission to the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. 18. During the face-to-face meeting in Geneva (May 17–19, 2017), the systematic review results and evidence profiles were presented and deliberated. The GRADE evidence-to-decision framework was used to formulate recommendations. 19. The guideline was drafted following the meeting, with final wording and justification of recommendations agreed upon. Peer reviewers' comments were addressed, and the guideline was revised accordingly. 20. The final guideline was approved after addressing all comments and ensuring no discrepancies among reviewers or development group members. External partners did not contribute to the guideline development process.
